name: Cerebral Palsy (CP)
summary: Cerebral palsy is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive disturbance in the developing brain (before, during or soon after birth). The brain lesion does not get worse, but musculoskeletal problems (contractures, hip displacement, bone deformity) can progress as the child grows.

looksLike: Delayed milestones, abnormal tone, toe walking, scissoring, asymmetry, persistent primitive reflexes.

Ask the family about birth history, milestones, current function at home and school, seizures, feeding, pain, sleep, equipment, previous treatment (botulinum toxin, surgery), and the child's and family's goals.
redFlags: New hip pain, reduced abduction, asymmetry
Pain or swelling after minor trauma in a non-walking child
Coughing and choking with meals, chest infections
firstSteps: Choose interventions with evidence for those goals; review every few months.
Monitor hips and contractures as the child grows.

measures: GMFM, goal attainment scaling, range, gait video, participation measures.

mistakes: Passive stretching alone has limited evidence for long-term contracture prevention. Combine with active use, standing, positioning and orthoses.
pearls: In paediatrics, the family is part of the team. Goals should reflect what matters in the child's daily life: playing with friends, walking to class, sitting to eat. Use the ICF framework (body function, activity, participation, environment, personal factors).

book.title: Cerebral Palsy (CP)
book.lead: Working with children and families: function, participation and growth.

blocks.text: Cerebral palsy is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive disturbance in the developing brain (before, during or soon after birth). The brain lesion does not get worse, but musculoskeletal problems (contractures, hip displacement, bone deformity) can progress as the child grows. CP often comes with other problems: epilepsy, intellectual, vision, hearing, speech, feeding and behaviour difficulties.

rows: One side, arm usually more than leg
Both legs more than arms; often premature birth
Walks with limitations (long distances, uneven ground)
Walks with a hand-held mobility device
Self-mobility with limitations; may use powered mobility

blocks.text: The GMFCS level predicts gross motor development and guides goal setting and hip surveillance [Ref – to verify].

sections.title: B to C. Presentation and family interview

blocks.text: Delayed milestones, abnormal tone, toe walking, scissoring, asymmetry, persistent primitive reflexes. Ask the family about birth history, milestones, current function at home and school, seizures, feeding, pain, sleep, equipment, previous treatment (botulinum toxin, surgery), and the child's and family's goals.

blocks.label: TEACHER'S VOICE
body: In paediatrics, the family is part of the team. Goals should reflect what matters in the child's daily life: playing with friends, walking to class, sitting to eat. Use the ICF framework (body function, activity, participation, environment, personal factors).

sections.title: D to E. Examination and measures

rows: Modified Ashworth or Modified Tardieu Scale
Spasticity; Tardieu compares slow and fast stretch angles
Range of motion: hip abduction, popliteal angle, ankle dorsiflexion with knee straight and bent (Silfverskiöld)
Hip surveillance; done regularly in GMFCS III to V [Ref – to verify]

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: New hip pain, reduced abduction, asymmetry
Pain or swelling after minor trauma in a non-walking child
Coughing and choking with meals, chest infections

steps: **Confirm the diagnosis is not progressive** (regression is a red flag).
**Choose interventions** with evidence for those goals; review every few months.
**Monitor hips and contractures** as the child grows.

rows: Practice of real tasks, high repetition [Ref – to verify]
Botulinum toxin plus stretching, casting, orthoses (medical team decides the drug)
Positioning, standing programs, night splints, serial casting

blocks.label: COMMON STUDENT TRAP
body: Passive stretching alone has limited evidence for long-term contracture prevention [Ref – to verify]. Combine with active use, standing, positioning and orthoses.

blocks.text: Functional electrical stimulation and hydrotherapy may support goals in selected children. Choose based on goals, not habit.
GMFM, goal attainment scaling, range, gait video, participation measures.

items: **Is CP a progressive brain disease?** No, the brain lesion is non-progressive, but musculoskeletal problems can progress with growth.
**Why is GMFCS useful?** It describes function, predicts motor development and guides surveillance.
**A child loses the ability to walk he previously had. What should you suspect?** A progressive condition; refer urgently.
**Which intervention for a child with hemiplegia and some hand function?** Constraint-induced or bimanual training.
**Why is hip surveillance important in GMFCS IV to V?** High risk of progressive hip displacement.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Classify CP by type, distribution and GMFCS.
Set family-centred goals and choose evidence-based interventions.
